title: The CEO’s Guide to Closing the AI-Knowledge Gap with Your Board
gist: BCG's inaugural 'Split Decisions: CEOs and Boards Survey' of 625 leaders finds that apparent CEO–board alignment on AI governance masks a real knowledge gap: 61% of CEOs say boards are rushing AI transformations, 37% say directors lack an informed view of how AI reshapes growth strategy, and 35% say boards overestimate AI's ability to replace rather than augment expertise. The article prescribes five CEO moves — personally owning the AI narrative, leading board upskilling, immersive off-cycle learning, differentiating augmentation vs. replacement, and standing up a 3–4 director AI transformation committee.

themes.theme: Split Decisions survey: illusory board alignment

insights.claim: BCG's inaugural 'Split Decisions: CEOs and Boards Survey' of 625 CEOs and directors found surface-level agreement on AI governance, implementation and value creation that conceals a fundamental disconnect in underlying AI understanding.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
entities: Split Decisions: CEOs and Boards Survey
insights.so_what: Governance-quality disclosures on AI are likely to be cosmetic; treat board-level 'AI alignment' claims in proxy statements as unverified until execution shows up in results.
insights.quote: On the surface, CEOs and directors appear largely aligned on AI governance, implementation, and value creation. But beneath that apparent consensus lies a fundamental disconnect

insights.claim: Three-quarters of board members rate their own AI understanding as on par with or better than their peers, while CEOs report that many of those same directors cannot distinguish AI hype from reality or calibrate how fast AI creates value.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Self-assessed AI competence at the board level is systematically inflated, so director AI credentials should be discounted when judging a company's capacity to oversee large AI capex.
insights.quote: three-quarters of board members rate their understanding of AI as on par with or better than their peers

insights.claim: 61% of CEOs surveyed by BCG believe their boards are rushing AI transformations.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Board-driven urgency is a plausible source of overspend and premature scaling of AI pilots — a margin risk in enterprises where the board, not management, sets the AI pace.
insights.quote:
61%

of CEOs believe boards are rushing AI transformations.

insights.claim: 35% of CEOs say their boards overestimate AI's ability to replace expertise rather than augment it.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Headcount-reduction guidance justified by AI may be board-driven optimism rather than operational reality; expect slippage between announced AI-driven cost saves and realized ones.
insights.quote:
35%

of CEOs believe boards overestimate AI’s ability to replace expertise rather than augment it.

insights.claim: 37% of CEOs say their boards lack an informed view of how AI is reshaping growth strategy.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Roughly a third of large-company boards are not equipped to price AI-driven changes in the path to growth, raising the odds of misallocated strategic investment.
insights.quote:
37%

of CEOs say boards lack an informed view of how AI is reshaping growth strategy.

themes.theme: Governance failure modes and CEO tenure risk

insights.claim: An unaddressed CEO–board understanding gap on AI stalls decision-making, weakens investment choices, and derails the transition from promising AI pilots to enterprise-scale value.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: The pilot-to-scale conversion rate — the key metric for enterprise AI monetization — is framed here as a governance problem, not a technology one.
insights.quote: Left unaddressed, this understanding gap can stall decision-making, weaken investment choices, and derail the journey from promising AI pilots to enterprise-scale value.

insights.claim: Directors frustrated with the pace of an AI transformation tend to become heavy-handed and start making decisions for the CEO, shifting effective control of strategy from management to the board.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Watch for boards seizing AI decision rights as an early governance red flag; it usually precedes erratic capital allocation and management turnover.
insights.quote: Board members who feel frustrated with the pace of an AI transformation can become heavy-handed and start making decisions for the CEO, with significant consequences for future competitiveness.
insights.locator: Why CEOs Must Close the Understanding Gap Now

insights.claim: Boards that judge a CEO insufficiently aggressive on AI begin questioning whether the company has the right leadership for an AI-first future, making perceived AI ambition a driver of CEO succession risk.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: CEO changes at large incumbents through this cycle should increasingly be read as AI-narrative events, not just performance events.
insights.quote: may question whether the company has the right leadership to steward the company successfully into an AI-first future
insights.locator: Why CEOs Must Close the Understanding Gap Now

themes.theme: Five-move CEO playbook for board AI literacy

insights.claim: BCG argues the CEO — not the CTO or an outside expert — should personally convey to the board what AI means for value creation strategy, competitive advantage, operating model, leadership expectations, and risk.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: A five-part checklist for auditing whether a company's public AI story is strategy or theater — if a CEO can only speak to tooling, the transformation is likely unanchored.
insights.locator: Move 1: Personally envision and articulate the AI strategy

insights.claim: BCG managing director Kristy Ellmer frames the core AI strategy test as separating where a company is merely keeping up from where AI actually creates competitive advantage — absent that distinction, AI adoption looks like implementation for its own sake.
insights.speaker: Kristy Ellmer
insights.so_what: Use the keeping-up vs. advantage split to screen corporate AI spend: parity spending is a cost line, advantage spending is the only part that should earn a multiple.
insights.quote: Where are we just keeping up, and where is AI actually creating competitive advantage? Otherwise, it can look like you’re implementing AI just for the sake of doing it.
insights.locator: Move 1: Personally envision and articulate the AI strategy

insights.claim: BCG managing director Julie Bedard recommends CEOs personally run hands-on AI upskilling sessions for their boards, demonstrating current tools rather than delegating director education to technology leaders or external experts.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Signals demand for CEO-level, tool-specific AI enablement — a services and training revenue pool sitting above the usual IT-buyer budget.
insights.quote: is for the CEO to personally lead an AI upskilling session for their board to show them the latest AI tools and what they can do

insights.claim: Because board meetings rarely allow enough time or context, BCG prescribes off-cycle director immersion — visits to AI-first companies, customer discussions, competitor scans, and exposure to live AI use cases.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Implies rising traffic and reference-customer demand at AI-native firms as incumbent boards tour them — a soft indicator of enterprise AI pipeline.
insights.locator: Move 3: Plan immersive learning opportunities beyond board meetings

insights.claim: Ellmer recommends forming a temporary AI transformation committee of three or four technically stronger directors who go deep with management and represent the rest of the board, needed only for the few years spanning the transition.
insights.speaker: Kristy Ellmer
insights.so_what: New AI/transformation board committees are an observable, disclosable signal that a company is past AI rhetoric and into governance of actual spend.
insights.quote: It’s helpful to have three or four directors who have some expertise and who are going to get deeper in it with you
insights.locator: Move 5: Consider building an AI-savvy transformation committee

insights.claim: Boards are systematically more aggressive than CEOs about using AI to replace workers, and CEOs must push back by specifying where human judgement remains essential.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: The pressure for AI-driven headcount cuts is coming from the board, which suggests announced layoffs may run ahead of what operations can actually absorb.
insights.quote: Boards are often more aggressive about replacing workers, and CEOs need to help them understand where human judgement remains essential.
insights.locator: Move 4: Articulate a vision for AI augmentation vs. replacement

insights.claim: Bedard's prescribed fix is for CEOs to talk about AI in a differentiated way that separates work activities where AI substitutes for humans from those where it complements them, rather than treating AI as a single blanket capability.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Activity-level substitute/complement mapping is the right granularity for modeling which sectors actually see AI-driven margin expansion versus cost-neutral augmentation.
insights.quote: to clearly illustrate where AI can be a substitute for human work activities, and where it can complement human work
insights.locator: Move 4: Articulate a vision for AI augmentation vs. replacement

themes.theme: Concentrated AI decision burden on the CEO

insights.claim: BCG's survey found CEOs end up carrying more of the AI decision-making burden than either they or their boards believe they should, concentrating transformation risk in a single executive.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Key-person risk in AI transformations is understated — a CEO departure at a company mid-transformation is more disruptive than org charts imply.
insights.quote: CEOs often end up carrying more of the AI decision-making burden than either they or their boards believe they should, according to our survey.
insights.locator: Final Gut Check: Don’t Carry the AI Transformation Alone

insights.claim: BCG predicts the companies that pull ahead will be those where responsibility for AI transformation is shared across CEO, board, and senior leadership team operating from a common understanding of how AI creates value.
insights.speaker: Julie Bedard
insights.so_what: Distributed AI accountability — explicit AI mandates across the C-suite, not just a CEO or CAIO — is a screenable differentiator among AI-adopting incumbents.
insights.quote: The companies that pull ahead will be those where responsibility for AI transformation is shared
insights.locator: Final Gut Check: Don’t Carry the AI Transformation Alone
